model:claude|title:a claude code agent s.content_excerpt: An incident report. Setup: Claude Code 2.1.286 in auto mode, seven background subagents running in parallel, macOS, no sandbox. Incident date: 2026-10-28. All times are local (PDT) and come from the agents’ transcripts and the macOS unified log. At 16:23 on a Wednesday, my Mac started talking. Two synthetic voices, talking over each other, reading something like “type, agent turn complete, thread id… turn id, one”. Twenty seconds later they stopped. Nobody had typed a command. I had seven autonomous coding agents working in parallel, each closing a GitHub issue in its own git worktree. My first thought was that one of them had found its way to a voice AI somewhere on the internet. The truth was more mundane and, I think, more worrying. One agent had written a test with a one-line bug. When it ran the test, the bug launched real processes on my machine : two that spoke out loud, and two background workers built to upload data to my production server. Nothing was damaged. That was luck, not design. This post covers what happened, how I traced it, and why it convinced me that autonomous agents need sandboxes by default. I build an observability tool for long-running AI agents. To move faster, I was running Claude Code in auto mode: one session launched seven background subagents, each assigned a GitHub issue. They wrote code, ran tests, and opened pull requests without me approving each step. They had no sandbox. Every agent ran as my user account, with my permissions, on my laptop. The agent at the center of this was implementing live capture : a hook that Claude Code or Codex calls after each turn, which starts a background worker to upload that session’s transcript. The bug was written, executed and fixed in 23 seconds. I noticed nearly four minutes later. The hook launches helper processes in the background. To test it without running anything, the tests passed in a fake launcher: a list that records each command instead of executing it. The fake starts as an empty list, and in Python an empty list is falsy. So spawn or _spawn threw the fake away and used the real launcher, which starts each command detached , in its own session, so it outlives the test. The test then “ran the user’s notification program”, with the program set to say and its argument set to the JSON that Codex sends after each turn: The fix was one line, spawn = _spawn if spawn is None else spawn . We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. model:glm|ver:5.3|title:glm 5 3 optimiza.content_excerpt: TL;DR: Long agentic contexts push GLM-5.3 against two limits on H200s: KV cache memory and prefill speed. We address both on 16 H200s, split into one prefill node and one decode node: Agentic workloads have long contexts that grow with every turn, which puts pressure on both GPU memory and prefill. On H200s, GLM-5.3's weights take up most of each GPU's memory, leaving little room for the KV cache of those long contexts. And because every turn adds more tool output and file contents to prefill, under load the prefill engines can become the bottleneck for the whole deployment. Part 1 showed how Hybrid HiSparse lets long contexts fit in an aggregated deployment on a single 8× H200 node. Prefill/decode disaggregation takes more than that. On the prefill node, we use PCP to speed up long prompts by parallelizing across the prompt's tokens. With MLA, however, this leaves every PCP rank holding a full copy of the KV cache, so we combine it with DCP to remove that replication. On the decode node, Hybrid HiSparse allows higher concurrency at long contexts. vLLM's new modular core ( Model Runner V2 ) makes composing all of this much easier. Neither scheme spreads one long prompt's attention work across the eight GPUs without also keeping its whole KV on each GPU that serves it. The next two sections address each half. PCP splits a prompt's queries across GPUs, and DCP splits its KV. In our 8× H200 prefill engine, PCP splits each prompt across the eight GPUs by token: every GPU computes the queries for one eighth of the prompt, with all 64 heads. A naive split would be unbalanced. Under causal attention a token attends to every token before it, so the GPU holding the end of the prompt would do far more work than the one holding the start. PCP instead cuts the prompt into 16 chunks and pairs them up: GPU takes chunk from the front and chunk from the back, so every GPU gets the same mix of cheap and expensive tokens (Figure 3 shows this as a V-shaped pattern across the eight GPUs). This is the load-balanced sharding from Context Parallelism for Scalable Million-Token Inference . Finally, each GPU's new KV is all-gathered, so every query can still attend to the full context. Figure 1 compares the two splits. PCP fixes both problems. Each GPU indexes only its own tokens, so the indexer is no longer replicated on every GPU and each GPU does an eighth of it. model:mistral|variant:large|title:day 0.content_excerpt: We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder. Supporting it took more than a model file. ML4 runs on vLLM's model runner V2 (MRV2) with breakable CUDA graphs. Its building blocks live in a new vllm/models/mistral/ package, and the work produced generic improvements to decode context parallelism (DCP), prefill context parallelism (PCP), DSpark, NIXL-based disaggregated serving and HiSparse host-memory KV offload. Mistral Large 4 support ships in the vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 Docker image, which also includes mistral-common 1.13. The commands below run vllm serve inside it: NVFP4 does not trade quality for speed. On multimodal, long-context, agentic coding, business automation and cyber evals it stays within 2.1 points of FP8 on every task, and the mean difference is −0.3 points. Token consumption is matched too: mean completion tokens stay within about 4% of FP8. It is also faster and lighter: at TP8, NVFP4 decodes 1.08–1.19x faster per token than FP8 without spec decoding (1.18–1.22x with DSpark) and holds ~1.5x the KV cache. Long context (DCP). Add --decode-context-parallel-size 8 to shard the latent KV cache across the 8 ranks. It requires the default FP8 KV cache. Multimodal. Pass --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": N}' to allow up to N images per prompt. For multi-node, disaggregated P/D and other tested configurations, see the Mistral Large 4 recipe . Sparse MLA + DSA indexer. ML4 reuses vLLM's sparse-MLA stack (FlashMLA sparse with the fp8_ds_mla latent cache, plus the sparse indexer with an FP8 indexer cache). ML4-specific differences are layered on top: shared-indexer layers that reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, an indexer with its own SSMax, and NoPE indexers on NoPE layers. Per token, the KV cache stores 47,136 bytes: 41,328 for the MLA latent and 5,808 for the indexer. Cross-layer KV sharing. Nine NoPE layers read the latent KV written by layer 35 instead of writing their own. We added kv_sharing_target_layer_name to MLAAttention and AttentionLayerBase . story|title:how ai agents shape experts.content_excerpt: When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call. We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded. Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead. Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed. Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment. We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world. story|title:how to build proactive alway.content_excerpt: Ever hear of the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon? It's when you learn a word for the first time, and suddenly start hearing it everywhere. I think the same principle applies in software engineering: You learn about a simple, but effective, design pattern, and then suddenly start seeing it everywhere. We're seeing this happen with proactive agents, where we've noticed that nearly all of your favorite emerging proactive agentic systems are powered by a very simple mechanism: Agent runs as cron tasks, leveraging a more than fifty-year old principle of operating systems for a very modern use case. The future belongs to proactive, always-on, ambient agents. Launches like Muse, Instinct, Dots, Claude Duet, Hone, and more reflect this. Crons power a few different capabilities that combine to make these agents proactive, personalized, and ambient — that is, they can perform tasks on their own, without being manually instructed. In this blog, we will go through the capabilities that crons unlock, the two core underlying parts you need in order to build agents like this, and then show examples of how you can do this in Managed Deep Agents . We’ve seen the impact crons can have. Proactivity is the new default for agent behaviour because of the breadth of new functions it unlocks. More than 70% of Managed Deepagent runs on LangSmith come from scheduled runs rather than a human typing a message. Crons, despite being a simple concept, unlock a few different behaviors that shape these proactive, always-on agents. Memory: A distinctive part of all these agents is that they remember facts about you over longer time horizons. Implementing this partially involves running a background job to condense previous conversations into a denser form of memory. This is colloquially called “dreaming”. Under the hood, this is just a cron that runs on some cadence (e.g. once a day) and updates long-term memory with any learnings from reflecting on the conversations. story|title:how we built our design agen.content_excerpt: The promo above was made by Content Studio, our design agent that can create videos, social graphics, recreated UI images, slide decks, and more from just a single prompt in Slack. Every asset the agent produces is written in code. Content Studio was built entirely in-house on Managed Deep Agents . It’s now one of the most widely used GTM agents within our company, but it didn’t start out that way. Early feedback was… not great. We've spent four months teaching Content Studio our taste and design principles, mostly by watching it get things wrong in front of the whole company. This post walks through how our GTM Engineering team worked with our design team to build Content Studio from scratch: what good design means to us, how we taught the agent our taste, and the harness that lets it make anything from a still to a launch film. LangChain moves fast. We have constant product launch campaigns, webinars, blogs and events. Each initiative needs assets, from blog headers and diagrams to decks, videos and ad creatives. Our design team was stretched thin, with repetitive requests crowding out more strategic and innovative work. As a lean startup, we needed a low-friction way for anyone at the company to create high-quality, on-brand work. To address these needs, we built Content Studio, a design agent that lives in Slack. A team member describes what they want and attaches accompanying content or briefs, and the agent returns finished, on-brand files. To build Content Studio, we needed three things: Managed Deep Agents gave us everything we needed to productionize Content Studio inside our company: a managed LangSmith Sandbox , integration with Slack, managed tools, scoped agent memory and scheduling agent runs. This allows a small team to spend its time on the design work, the skills, tools and Slack experience, instead of the plumbing. Before jumping into the build, let’s first address the debate of the century: can AI actually produce good design? The model was already good at execution and could write HTML and CSS, chart specs and animation timelines. However, it didn't have our context, so it reached for familiar patterns, what Anthropic calls “distributional convergence” . The result could look polished and still look like a hundred others, or be beautifully animated and never get its point across. story|title:omneum local text blind cont.content_excerpt: Text-blind context control plane for AI agents. Select high-utility context under token budgets. Omneum is an open-source context control plane for AI agents, built to optimize the evidence entering an LLM's context window. Agents accumulate context from retrieval, tools, memory, and previous sessions, but longer context windows don't guarantee better reasoning. Context rot can slowly degrade downstream answer accuracy even when the relevant information has already been retrieved. Provenance-aware graph inference: Iteratively computes source reliability and claim support across a bipartite graph, accounting for shared evidence origins and dependencies between sources. Context reconstruction: Selects original retrieved passages based on question relevance and incremental claim coverage within a token budget. Text-blind evaluation: Evaluates structured observations without reading source text strings or invoking an LLM judge. Local by default: Persists your agents' observations across sessions in a Context Graph , backed by SQLite or PostgreSQL. Compare retrieval-order packing with Omneum's claim-coverage selection under the same context budget. Packing chunks in retrieval order consumes 75 units while covering only two claims. Omneum retains two original chunks covering all four, using 32% less context capacity . Omneum uses a graph-based mathematical analysis, calculated from Observation objects, to estimate the structural reliability of sources and the support for claims found in retrieved context. Importantly, this analysis does not naively assume every source has derived its information independently. The same information often propagates across multiple sources. Without dependency tracking, five observations from different sources can be difficult to distinguish from five reports derived from the same upstream source. How much support should that claim receive? That depends partly on the reliability of the sources reporting it. But how do we determine the reliability of the sources? By looking at the claims they support. This definition seems circular, and it is. Nonetheless, it provides a well-defined notion of reliability that helps distinguish strongly supported context from weakly supported context. Of course claim-level scores are only useful for context selection if they can be mapped back to chunks. story|title:smarter cost controls for se.content_excerpt: At Databricks, our serverless compute usage has grown more than 3x in the past year, and thousands of customers now run mission critical notebooks, jobs, and pipelines on it. As adoption climbs, the question every platform team asks first only gets louder: how do we gain better visibility into serverless costs and keep the cost within our budget? Databricks customers running serverless SQL and Model Serving already attribute spend, govern access, and monitor consumption without touching a single cluster knob. We are now bringing that same functionality to serverless compute for notebooks, jobs, and pipelines. We are making serverless cost controls work the way platform teams already expect it to. On classic compute, cost control lived in the infrastructure. You capped spend by capping machines: node counts, instance types, autoscaling ranges, and cluster policies that fenced in what users could provision. The controls were required because you had to manage the infrastructure on your own. Serverless takes those knobs away, on purpose. Provisioning, scaling, and right-sizing infrastructure is the platform's burden now, handled by Databricks, which is a big part of the value. But cost control has to live somewhere, so it moves up a layer. Instead of attaching to machines, it attaches to people and workloads. Who is allowed to run serverless, how fast a workload is allowed to spend, and where the cost lands are the questions that matter now. Classic compute answered these with three tools: tags to attribute cost, entitlements to control access, and cluster size limits to cap spend. Serverless needs the same three. Two of them exist today, and the third is coming. Attribution starts with tags. On classic compute you tagged the cluster; on serverless you tag the compute, and every DBU that compute runs carries that tag through to billing. The same table answers the audit question you will want before you change anyone's access: who is actually running serverless today, and how much are they spending? That is one more query, ranked by consumption, and the full examples live in the system tables documentation. Availability: Serverless Compute tags for attribution is currently available in Beta . Observability is already available and customers can already monitor serverless cost with system tables on AWS , Azure , and Google Cloud . story|title:spinf serve inference server.content_excerpt: Bulk classification and decision inference on one GPU: the content is read once, every question about it is scored in the same pass. OpenAI-compatible, Apache 2.0 spinf-serve reads a piece of content once and answers many questions about it in the same pass. Each answer is a probability over the options you give, not generated text. It runs on one 24 GB NVIDIA GPU and serves an OpenAI-compatible API, the same API as the hosted spinf service. Apache 2.0. We built this engine for our own work: a daily market index read from millions of news articles, each article asked dozens of narrow, calibrated questions. A serving engine built for chat re-reads the content for every question and generates one token at a time, which made that job slow and expensive. spinf-serve lays every question out as a branch of one read of the content and packs many contents into one forward pass. Bulk classification is where it started and where it is strongest. The same mechanism is what is now called a decision model : a model that returns a probability over a fixed set of answers (yes or no, a label, a level) instead of a paragraph. Any open instruction model works this way in spinf-serve, and dedicated decision models run as they are. The hosted spinf API grew out of this engine; we are publishing it because people asked to run it on their own hardware. It is not a chat server. Nothing is generated unless you ask for it, and it is built for throughput rather than for the latency of a single request. Linux, an NVIDIA GPU with 24 GB and fp8 tensor cores (Ada, Hopper or Blackwell: RTX 4090 / 5090, L4, L40S, RTX 6000 Ada, H100), a driver supporting CUDA 13, Python 3.12. story|title:things that go beep in the n.content_excerpt: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.” Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold. At the Allen Telescope Array, DAQIRI , a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. CyberEther , a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including cuFFT and cuBLAS . Nexus , a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. story|variant:speech|title:introducing a.content_excerpt: Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do. Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive. In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap , we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model. Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device. Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer , Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen. It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine: The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer , SpeechTranscriber , DictationTranscriber , SpeechDetector , and AssetInventory , with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber: The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework. Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 . It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale. Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3 . It was more accurate in most of our measurements. All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence. Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover.
